hook.text: Data traveling across the internet can be intercepted. Without encryption, anyone on the path can read it.

buildup.text: TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts data in transit. It's the padlock icon in your browser.

discovery.text: Cloud providers enforce TLS for API calls. Your data is encrypted between your device and the cloud.

twist.text: TLS protects data between points — but at each endpoint, data is decrypted. Insiders can still see it.

climax.text: End-to-end encryption solves this: data stays encrypted from sender to receiver. Nobody in between can read it.

punchline.text: In transit means in danger. TLS is the shield.

quiz.question: What does TLS protect against?
options: Interception of data as it travels across networks
Physical theft of hard drives from data centers
Users choosing weak passwords for their accounts

details.summary: Encryption in transit protects data as it moves between clients and servers or between cloud services using protocols like TLS. Without it, attackers can intercept sensitive information through man-in-the-middle attacks on network traffic.
details.whyItMatters: Data crosses many network hops between users and cloud services. Encrypting traffic ensures confidentiality and integrity even on untrusted networks.
takeaways: TLS encrypts data moving between endpoints
Should be enforced for all internal and external traffic

faq.question: Is HTTPS enough for encryption in transit?
faq.answer: HTTPS via TLS protects client-to-server traffic, but service-to-service communication within the cloud also needs encryption. Mutual TLS authenticates both ends of a connection, and service meshes can automate encryption for all internal microservice traffic.

faq.question: What TLS version should be used?
faq.answer: TLS 1.2 is the minimum acceptable version, and TLS 1.3 is preferred for its improved security and performance. Older versions like TLS 1.0 and 1.1 have known vulnerabilities and should be disabled in all cloud configurations.
